name: lfe
desc: Concurrent Lisp for the Erlang VM
why: A Lisp dialect running on the Erlang VM, a genuinely unusual pairing worth an afternoon of exploring.

brief.what_it_is: LFE (Lisp Flavoured Erlang) is a Lisp-syntax front-end to the Erlang compiler, so LFE code runs on the BEAM virtual machine. You give it LFE source, either typed into its REPL, saved as a script, or compiled as a module, and it produces ordinary Erlang-compatible code that can call and be called by normal Erlang modules. It includes a REPL and evaluator for interactive work, plus lfescript for one-off scripts. Its data types are Erlang's: lists, tuples, maps, atoms, and binaries, with strings being lists of integers.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage tagline is "Taking the syntax out of distributed systems programming", and the README says LFE is a lisp syntax front-end to the Erlang compiler, so the idea is to give Erlang/OTP's concurrency, distribution, and fault-tolerance machinery a Lisp surface syntax.
brief.how_it_works: LFE source is read by an LFE reader and compiled through the Erlang compiler toolchain into BEAM bytecode, so it is interchangeable with Erlang modules at runtime. Macros are compile-time only, except in the REPL, and they are unhygienic but scoped, with no gensym, because the author says that would be unsafe for code shared with remote nodes. The homepage also describes OTP behaviours (gen_server, supervisors) being used directly from LFE syntax.

brief.install_notes: Requires Erlang/OTP installed with the erl binary on PATH. Build from source with git clone, then make compile; run tests with make tests. make install copies lfe, lfec, lfedoc and lfescript to /usr/local/bin by default (PREFIX overrides this) and installs man pages (MANINSTDIR overrides). The README's install list omits lfeexec, lfe-test and lfe-first-try, which Homebrew also ships, so their purpose is not documented in what I read. Docker is an alternative (docker pull lfex/lfe). No accounts or API keys are mentioned. Libraries come from hex.pm, and the README's Slack invite and Erlang Forums are listed for community help.
brief.standout: Lisp-2 semantics (separate function and variable namespaces) on the BEAM, with Erlang-style pattern matching in defun arguments, lets you write Lisp macros that call Erlang's OTP directly. The author's choice to drop gensym and accept unhygienic macros, because code is shared with remote nodes, is an unusual trade-off, stated plainly in the homepage text.
brief.status: maintained. Evidence: the README has an active CI badge and Hex.pm version and download badges, documents a full release process (make tags, make publish), and the REPL banner in the README shows LFE v2.2.1 on OTP 26. I did not see a dated last release or last commit, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: Needs a working Erlang/OTP install, with erl on PATH, before LFE will build or run. The README gives no Windows instructions, and I saw none, so platform support is unclear. Macros are unhygienic (no gensym), so hygiene is the author's responsibility. The homepage describes the SICP LFE edition as only partly complete. The homepage's '40% of the world's telecommunications' claim is marketing copy I did not verify. The homepage is largely promotional, so the README and code examples are the more reliable guide. The homebrew caveats field was empty.
